newsitem.title: USA: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The Federal Reserve opted on Tuesday to keep interest rates unchanged amid signs that the see-saw economy was settling down to steady growth as 1996 draws to a close.

The decision had been widely expected, but it nevertheless was greeted with relief on Wall Street, where the Dow Jones industrial average of blue-chip shares closed the day 39.98 points higher at 6,308.33.

Analysts were divided over the outlook for short-term rates in 1997, though few saw any pressing need for the central bank's key Federal Open Market Committee to alter its interest rate policy soon. The panel next meets on Feb. 4-5.

"As the Fed looks forward into the first half of 1997, there is no sign of imbalance that could throw the economy off the intended path," said David Resler, chief economist at Wall Street broker Nomura Securities International.
"Until it becomes clear the economy is veering off course, it's impossible to predict the direction or the timing of the next Fed move," he added.
Recent statistics have portrayed an economy with pockets of weakness and strength that remains surprisingly free of any inflationary tendencies more than 5-1/2 years into an expansion.
After stripping out volatile food and energy costs, consumer prices rose at a modest year-on-year rate of 2.6 percent in November.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan earlier this month called inflation "low," although he added that its future course remained uncertain.

Labour markets are tight and unemployment low, raising the risk of stepped-up wage demands. But product markets are, in Greenspan's words, "comfortable," indicating no shortages that could lead to higher prices.
After cutting rates by a quarter percentage point in January, the Fed has held policy steady as economic growth has first waxed and then waned.
The federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans now stands at 5.25 percent. The discount rate that the Fed charges the banks is 5 percent.
Analysts said the Fed's next move will depend on the course that the economy and inflation takes in the new year.

If the economy starts growing much faster than its presumed long-term cruising speed of roughly 2.25 percent and inflation picks up, the Fed is likely to raise rates. Growth much slower than that would make a rate cut more likely.
The economy expanded by 2 percent in the third quarter. Growth in the current quarter is expected to slightly better that rate, helped by a pick-up in consumer spending in the run-up to Christmas.
The steady Fed stance does not mean that policymakers, who are paid to worry about the economy, have no concerns.
Some fret that Wall Street stock prices may be too high. Others worry that unemployment may be too low. But none seem concerned enough to alter policy anytime soon.

Greenspan warned earlier this month that the Fed needed to be wary when "irrational exuberance" infected stock and other asset markets because of the risk of a subsequent crash that could damage the economy.
Some of the froth though has gone out of the stock market since then, as investors have cashed in part of their profits, pushing share prices lower.
Greenspan also has his eyes on the tight labour market for signs of stepped-up wage demands that could lead to higher inflation. So far, that has not proved to be the case.
The unemployment rate rose to 5.4 percent in November, from 5.2 percent in October, easing some of the pressures in the labour market.
